panels.text: ENIAC was 80 feet long, 8 feet tall, and weighed 30 tons. It had 17,468 vacuum tubes, 70,000 resistors, 10,000 capacitors, 6,000 switches, and 5 million hand-soldered joints. It consumed 150 kilowatts of power. There's a myth it dimmed the lights of an entire Philadelphia neighborhood — almost certainly false. What IS true: it generated enough heat to warm the building in winter.

In 1943, the U.S. Army needed artillery firing tables — charts telling gunners how to aim. Human teams, mostly women mathematicians officially called "computers," were doing this work by hand. They were months behind. J. Presper Eckert (24, engineering prodigy) and John Mauchly (36, visionary physicist) proposed building an electronic calculator. The Army, desperate, funded the project.

panels.prompt: Close-up of hands plugging thick cables into a massive patch panel covered in hundreds of connection points, 1940s setting. A woman in professional 1940s attire is carefully rearranging cables and flipping switches on ENIAC's programming panels. The panel is a dense wall of sockets, cables, and switches. Focused, methodical work. Warm lighting, dramatic shadows. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, orange accent highlights

panels.text: But there was a catch. To "program" ENIAC, you didn't write code. You physically rewired the machine. Rearranging cables, setting switches, plugging connections — a process that could take days or weeks. The computation itself took seconds. Setting it up took forever.

panels.caption: A vacuum tube is an electronic switch: current flows = 1, no current = 0. That's binary.

panels.lab_description: Switches can do math? See it for yourself — build a calculator from nothing but ON/OFF switches!

panels.text: ENIAC was built by Eckert and Mauchly. But who PROGRAMMED it? Not the men. The job of making ENIAC actually work was given to six women — and then history forgot their names.
